conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the surgery team. You’re just arriving from the recovery area after we reopened and cleaned out the top part of your abdominal incision and removed a piece of suture that was acting like a foreign body. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sore and kind of worried. Why wouldn’t it heal? It kept draining even though the skin looked closed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common pattern when there’s a small cavity underneath the skin—sometimes it tracks deeper and keeps producing drainage. In your case we were concerned there might be retained suture material irritating the tissue, so we reopened the area, debrided the unhealthy tissue, and removed the suture we found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t like the G-tube itself causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This was in the upper part of your midline incision rather than the tube site itself. The tube is still in place, and we’ll resume your tube feeds once you’re fully awake and comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need another big surgery if it doesn’t close?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our goal is to avoid that. By removing the foreign body and cleaning the wound, we’re giving it the best chance to heal from the inside out. The key part at home will be packing the wound with dressing twice a day so it doesn’t seal over too early on top.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts. What are you giving me for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use oral pain medicine as needed—an oxycodone-acetaminophen liquid is ordered for breakthrough pain. We’ll also keep an eye on nausea and make sure you can drink fluids and take your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have an infection? They mentioned cellulitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There was concern for infection around the wound given the persistent drainage and irritation. After cleaning it out, we’re treating you with antibiotics to cover skin bacteria—at discharge you’ll take amoxicillin-clavulanate for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I eat? And can I restart my tube feeds today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll advance your diet as you tolerate it, and we’ll resume your tube feeds as well. We’ll also check your blood sugars while you’re here since your feeding plan is part of keeping them stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been okay lately with the tube feeds. Will this wound thing mess that up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shouldn’t. Today you’ve tolerated restarting feeds, and your blood sugars have stayed stable. We’ll keep your usual regimen and home medications unless we tell you otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you show me what the dressing is supposed to look like? I’m nervous I’ll do it wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. The nurse will do the next change with you watching, and we’ll have you practice. The idea is to gently pack the wound so it fills the space, then cover it with a clean dry dressing. You’ll do that twice daily at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me call you or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or return right away for fever over 101.5, shaking chills, worsening redness or swelling, increasing or foul-smelling drainage, worsening pain, vomiting where you can’t keep fluids or meds down, chest pain, or new shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight you stayed afebrile and your vital signs were stable. How’s your pain this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than yesterday. Still tender when I move. The tube feeds didn’t bother me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we want to hear. Your heart and lungs look good, your abdomen is soft, and the dressing is clean and dry. Since you’re tolerating diet and tube feeds and your pain is controlled with oral medication, we’re planning discharge today with home services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on any special restrictions? I have kids at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest and walk several times a day, but avoid heavy lifting until you see your surgeon in follow-up. Also don’t drive or operate machinery while you’re taking the narcotic pain medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I leaving with? I don’t want to mess up my usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume your regular home medications. New or changed items: amoxicillin-clavulanate by mouth every 12 hours for 7 days, oxycodone-acetaminophen liquid as needed for pain, and mupirocin nasal ointment twice daily for 30 days. Everything else stays the same unless your outpatient doctors adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And follow-up is with Dr. __, right? If the drainage comes back, I call sooner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—follow up with Dr. __ in clinic as scheduled, and call sooner if you notice increasing drainage, redness, swelling, fever, or worsening pain. You’re doing well to go home today.
